utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. It is nice to be back after a long time off. I hope both counsel have received the scheduling order for the witnesses appearing on the 28th and 29th week. I think you will have had the scheduling order by now, because we have received them from the prosecution. We are sitting all days of the week from Monday, through Thursday and Friday, all five days a week. We will be sitting for the period. Can we have the witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. Our next witness, your Honour, was supposed to be a protected witness to be identified as Witness C for the public and the media. However, he is now willing to testify in open court without any protective measures. So the prosecution withdraws the request for protection. We will call him as Mr. Vaso Dordic as our next witness. He was one of the persons from the videotape from Belgrade TV shown by the defence on Wednesday, 11th June. Before calling this witness into the court, may I request your Honours to allow the prosecution -- the prosecution believes that a particular issue has to be brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber. It will take a short time, but may I ask your Honours to allow me to do this before the witness comes and in private session, please, because of the confidentiality of the issue? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can do that. Let us go into private session for the time being for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is it already private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: No. Inform them. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: (In open session) (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness. MR. VASO DORDIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Vaso Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, you just read out a declaration about saying the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Do you understand the meaning of that declaration and do you understand what telling the truth means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 9th October 1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Born in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, what education did you receive? I mean, what kind of schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary school and too the high school and then later the fire-fighting course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many years did you attend elementary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elementary school, I went to elementary school for eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What kind of school did you attend after elementary school exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to -- it was a railroad school called Vaso Miskin Crni in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: For how many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What subjects did you study in this technical vocational school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had the subject of fire-fighting. That was the main subject in this technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you do after these years in technical school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have a job right away, so I worked as a construction worker for six months, and then later I moved to another company and I worked on painting bridges. After that I got a job and I went to work in Rilovats in the railroad yards, and I was there a fireman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which capacity did you serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the army on 15th March 19th 1988 to Sviliniz. I was there 2 months and 22 days. Then I was transferred to Belgrade to the bakery. I served as a baker in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, how did it happen that you were hired as a fireman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My late father worked in Sarajevo, and so it was through him that I found a job. It was sort of like a privilege.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you work as a fireman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in Rilovats in the technical station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did you work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked there two years, until the war broke out in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say: what did you normally do during your working day while you were a fireman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During a regular working day I worked in the office. I had a shift of five people and I was the shift commander, and sometimes I went out in the field. I would check on the trains that were arriving in that station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Dordic. Where did you live at the time -- in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1992 I lived in the village of Zukici near Bradina, about three and a half kms out of Konjic, between Konjic and Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With whom did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my father, my mother and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say the name of your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother's name is Veseljko Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when Bradina was affected by the armed conflict and then your village, Zukici, was affected by the armed conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately the day when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first attack on Bradina was conducted on 12th May. Later on 22nd May there was another one, and then Bradina fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At that time I was at home throughout this period. I was working in the field and I never went away until the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So there was a time when you were arrested in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say when were you arrested in July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 12th July, St Peter's Day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain the circumstances of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested in such a way that the neighbours came, knocked on the door, and they told myself, my brother and my late parents to come out, and at that time Dordic Gojka, Borka, Radojka and Savo and Sofija and Marija Dordic were all arrested at the same time, and this was all done by our neighbours: Redzo Ljevo, Redzo Balic, Hajrudin Rizvanovic, Elvedin and Mohammed Niksic. One of them had a trucking company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did these people arresting you belong to any military unit, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time they were all members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did they wear uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did; some did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And could you see any insignia on the uniforms of the ones who wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had insignia on the arms, and they were the TO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, were you told why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any weapon at the time of your arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not own any weapons. I was not a member of any such party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you in any way take part in the defence of your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was at home all the time. I was working with my neighbours. I was working in the field and I was trying to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately at what time of the day you were arrested on July 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I only know that it was St Peter's Day, that it was 12th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So what happened to you after you were arrested? Where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was first taken to the motel in Konjic and then from there I was then transferred to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With which vehicle were you transferred to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The vehicle was a Tam. Mohammed Niksic took me first to the motel and then from the motel to Celebici in a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately at what time did you arrive at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left home around 12.00 and so I arrived in Celebici around 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean 2.00 in the night, 2.00 am or 2.00 pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 2.00 am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you arrived at Celebici in the night between 12th and 13th July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many prisoners were together with you in the vehicle which transported you to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all of us from Zukici that were first -- that had first been brought to the motel. All of us then went to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, would you now tell us in detail what happened to you right after your arrival at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we got to Celebici they separated women and children, and myself, my brother and my late father were all taken to Number 6, to the hangar, that same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there other prisoners inside Hangar 6 when you first arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of people there. When the day came, I saw that there were many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say very approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 200, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say where exactly inside the hangar did you sleep the first night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That first night I was taken to Number 6 and I was put near the door, the entrance to the hangar. It was first me, then my brother and then my late father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you were close to one another inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one next to the other inside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And close to the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Then what happened the very next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next morning three people came and said: "Come on out, you who came out last night." So my father, myself and my brother Veseljko came out, and outside -- and the person who -- the person who --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Speak slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person who introduced himself to my late father said that his name was Zdravko Mucic and that he was the camp commander. That morning there were three persons there who introduced themselves. He said that he was the camp commander and said that his name was Pavo Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the one -- of these three people, the one who asked: "Who are the new ones who came yesterday night?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Pavo Mucic who asked the question: "Who are the new ones who arrived last night from Zukici?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When and how did you get to know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Pavo Mucic the first time and I found out his name when he introduced himself to us, to myself, to my brother Veseljko and my late father Jelenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you know that his name was Mucic? Did he introduce himself with his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He introduced himself and he said his own name. He said that he was Pavo Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know the names of the other two people who were with him in this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I later met Hazim Delic and Landzo Zenga. As I spent time in the prison, I learned who they were later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So my question is: who are the other two people who were with Mr. Mucic the first morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That first morning there was Landzo Zenga and Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. What did Mr. Mucic tell your father exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mucic said to my father that he was letting him go home and that the two of us had to stay to make a statement and that we would follow my late father soon, that we would be released. He said that we had to stay for a couple of days to make a statement, and then he would let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delic say something on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion Delic kept silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dordic, what happened to you and your brother that morning right after the release of your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That morning we were taken back to Number 6. My father was released. We had to go back to Hangar Number 6, and at that moment a guard walked in, whom I didn't know, and he took me and my brother out and he beat us, first my father on the side of Number 6, and he hit my brother with a knife here. (Indicating). He split his eyebrows. Later on I learned while I was in prison that the man in question was Landzo Zenga. I learned his name from the other inmates. They called each other by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did exactly Zenga do to you and your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga forced me to do push-ups. Then he lit a fuse on me. Then he forced us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am speaking about this first morning, this first morning right after the release of your father.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He beat us on that occasion that very first morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With what did Zenga beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He beat us with his feet, that is his boots, and his rifle butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you were beaten by Zenga, by Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was not. It was not the only time. He beat us later again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many times did Mr. Landzo beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo beat me every day while I was in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say -- did Mr. Landzo say anything while beating you in all these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. He would just come into the hangar, take me out, and he'd shout: "Come out. Come outside." Then he would begin to beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. So can you describe the physical characteristics of Building Number 6, Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building of Hangar Number 6 was as follows. It was steel sheets outside and inside you could see the steel structures. The beams were in steel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How big was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 27, 28 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you always maintain the same position inside Hangar 6, the one near the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was always in the same position, right next to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And did your brother also maintain the same position near the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were non-stop together. We never separated. We lay next to the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sir, approximately how long did you stay in Hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Hangar Number 6 for four months and then I was transferred to the sports hall in Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how were the conditions of life in Hangar 6, food, drinking water, sleeping facilities, toilet facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions in Number 6 were terrible. We received food once a day, sometimes twice, and water only once a day. We slept on the concrete floor in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say how were the toilet facilities, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a WC outside and at night there was a bucket right next to the door, which was used during the night for urination. Then in the morning we had to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you allowed to go outside during the day to urinate outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were allowed; some were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any period of time during which you did not have any food for the whole day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were periods when we had no food for two days in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about drinking water? Was the supply of drinking water stable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have drinking water regularly. We had small quantities, very small quantities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, were you ever interrogated during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During my stay in Celebici I was interrogated only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was interrogated after five or ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say where in the camp did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at the command building, near the entrance, at the very entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was anybody else interrogated in the same occasion as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day only my father, Veseljko Dordic, was taken for interrogation with me, just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I heard "father"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who called you out of the hangar? Who called you and your brother out of the hangar and brought you to the command building on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion the guard Zenga took us down to the command building to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was interrogated first, you or your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken in first and my brother stayed outside in front of the building. He was standing in the open air facing the dispensary and with his back turned to the command building. I was the first to be interrogated. I was the first to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say in which room of the command building were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a room facing the dispensary. The windows were facing the dispensary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By whom were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic was there and Hazim Delic and Ismeta was typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you sitting at a table during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was sitting next to a table and I was interrogated by Hazim Delic. He was speaking and I kept quiet and Ismeta was typing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you see the window of the room during the time of your interrogation? I mean, was the window in front of you? Could you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The window was in front of me. The window was facing another building, which was called the dispensary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What else could you see through the window, if anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see Landzo Zenga beating my brother using his rifle on his body while I was making the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How were you treated during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was treated in such a way that I was sitting on a chair next to the table and Hazim Delic took out his pistol and pointed it against my forehead and hit me with it, telling me to confess whatever he was saying, and Ismeta was typing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Delic sitting at the table during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What was his position inside the room then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was next to me. He was standing next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he simply hold the pistol against you? What did he say else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wasn't saying anything. He was just pointing the pistol against me, and he was telling me to confess. He hit me on the head. He also slapped me. My nose started bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, was Mr. Mucic sitting at the table during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo Mucic throughout my interrogation was in the office and he was watching. Later on he went out and he didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean, was he sitting at the table during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what was his position on that chair inside the room with respect to the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to the window he was sitting on the side. He was looking through the window. He was looking outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mucic say anything during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you accused of anything specific during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the interrogation, yes, they accused me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because on 11th July the policemen were killed in Duboki Potok between Repovci and Bradina. They claimed I was the one who had killed them and that is apparently why I was taken to prison. Hazim Delic was forcing me to confess to this, that I had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have to sign any piece of paper, any record, after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the statement. I wanted to sign in Latin script and he said: "No. You are a Cetnik. You have to sign in Cyrillic alphabet." I had to sign that statement in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, was that a long interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened right after your interrogation was finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I was taken out and my brother was brought in, Veseljko Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally see Veseljko entering the room for his own interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because we met at the door, the door leading into the room where I was, and then he was interrogated and I had to turn my back against the window and I was facing the dispensary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean that during Veseljko's interrogation you had the same position as he had during yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was sitting on the same chair that I was sitting at when I was in the room, but we met at the door, at the entrance into the room where I was interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, did you personally suffer any other physical maltreatment besides what you already said during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you please describe in detail every single incident concerning you personally, possibly in chronological order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one day Landzo Zenga came in and he said to me that I had to do push-ups, ten push-ups. Then after the ten he started beating me. Then I do two push-ups and then again he kicked me with his soldier's boots here on the side (indicating) and that was repeated every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Any other incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he would beat me also with his rifle butt. He would set light to a fuse on me. Then he forced me to do oral sex with my own brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe in detail one by one these incidents? Let us start with the incident of the fuse. Can you describe in detail what happened with this fuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With this fuse he would take a piece of it this long --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "he" was taking, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo Zenga. Zenga took this piece of slow-burning fuse roughly this long and then he -- I apologise. Can I use my own words?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You can use your own words, certainly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wound it round my anus. He put one end inside and the other round my penis. Then there was a piece sticking out here. (Indicating). Then he lit it. I have a scar there from this fuse. He did this in front of all the prisoners in the hangar, in the middle of the hangar near the door. All the prisoners could see what Zenga was doing to me, how he set light to this fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did he set light to this fuse? With a match; with a lighter? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a lighter. With a lighter he lit this slow-burning fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean the end of the fuse that was coming out from the trousers on your back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The part that was sticking out from the back, he set light to it, and the fuse started burning, and then a man ran up to me. I don't know who it was. He put it out. Then somebody called out somebody outside. They were calling "Hazim, Hazim." They put it out. I still have the scar there from this fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please explain better where were Mr. Landzo while the fuse was burning after lighting -- after putting fire on the fuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo was next to me. He was standing next to me all the time. I tried to put it out, but he wouldn't let me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How could that happen that another person came and put the fire out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards outside were saying: "Hazim, Hazim." He ran out, closed the door of Number 6. Then other people came up to me and put out the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "he ran out", who do you mean by "he ran out"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga ran out of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, could you describe better how did Mr. Landzo wrap the fuse around you? Was that while you were dressed or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He ordered me to take off my trousers and my pants and then he wrapped the fuse round my body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly how did he wrap it round your body? Describe better without being embarrassed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I stand up and show you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (Indicating). A part of the fuse was right here, under here (indicating) and then back. Then he put an end into my anus, and then the other end was showing up here. Then later he forced me to put on my knickers and my trousers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So you were saying a while ago something about oral sex. Could you please now describe this other incident about oral sex in detail, please, without being embarrassed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. One day Zenga entered Number 6 and he said -- he told me and my brother: "Get up." We got up and we were there right next to the door. He ordered us to take off our trousers. First my brother took off his and then he forced me to kneel down in front of my brother and to put into my mouth his genitals. So then he -- we changed and while I was holding my brother's sexual organ, he forced us to do that for about two or three minutes. Then he had to -- then I had to get up and my brother had to kneel down in front of me and do the same thing, and all prisoners saw this. It was done in front of all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean this took place inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the hangar in front of all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Landzo say anything while doing this to you and your brother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo said to me in front of all the prisoners: "See what the Serbian brothers and Cetniks are doing. That's what they would do to me too." Those were the words of Zenga Landzo in front of all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, going back for a moment to the incident of the fuse, did Mr. Landzo say anything during that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He didn't say anything to me. He only lit up this fuse and kept silent and looked at me. I started jumping up and down when this fuse started burning and I tried to put it out, but he would not allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you have any other incident you can describe concerning you personally? I mean, did you ever suffer any other physical maltreatment besides the ones you described so far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later Landzo Zenga had a dug-out where he spent his free time and he would take me there. He would put a gas mask on me and he would beat me in this dug-out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Sir, what physical consequences are still visible in your body after all these incidents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After all these events what I have in terms of visible signs are my teeth are knocked out because he was putting his rifle in there, and then I also have the scar from this fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dordic, did you personally eyewitness any mistreatment of any other prisoner while you were in Celebici? Would you please tell us? Did you eyewitness other incidents concerning our prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Also Landzo Zenga was setting fire on Bendjo. He had a tin with him. There was a flame coming out. I don't know what it was. He was heating the knife on it. Then he would put it against his shin and he would put it against his body, this heated knife. Also there was Mirko Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Wait a minute, please, Mr. Dordic. About this incident concerning Dusko Bendo, where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened in Hangar Number 6 in front of all the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After he burned out the fuse on my body, shortly thereafter he did it to Dusko Bendjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You can go ahead. You were talking about Mirko Dordic. What were you telling us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He put the heated pincers in his ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "he put", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga put the pincers, heated ones, into the ear of Dusko Bendjo and he also put it on his tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean Dusko Bendjo or Mirko Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to Mirko Dordic that he put this heated pincers and to Dusko Bendjo he was placing a heated knife against his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did the incident concerning Mirko Dordic happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was also in the hangar, in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally eyewitness any mistreatment of any other prisoners beside these ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other things. They would take people out at night or the day, and they would beat them. We were even beaten inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know anything because of direct knowledge about the circumstances of the death of any prisoner inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present when Keljo was killed. That morning Keljo and I took out the bucket, the one where people were relieving themselves. Padalovic ordered us to take it out and to clean up. We took it out to the toilet behind the hangar and then we cleaned it out and we washed it, the urine where we had -- we hosed it down with water and then Padalovic called: "Keljo, Keljo, come over here." They lit up a cigarette and I stayed at the door. When they lit up cigarettes, Keljo started towards the hangar --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Keljo started towards the hangar Padalovic aimed at him. I was looking, watching it all. He aimed his rifle. He put it against a step and he said: "Keljo, don't run. I'll kill you." Keljo just shrugged off and Keljo started running, and then Padalovic fired and he killed Keljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally see Keljo falling to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He fell down, his face to the ground, on the concrete, and I was standing at the door. I had not yet come inside. So I was 5 or 6 metres -- it was 5 or 6 metres away from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you personally see where Mr. Klimenta was reached by the shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Keljo was hit here in the small of the neck. I think he was hit right there (indicating), because blood was coming out of his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean you saw blood coming out from that part of the head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just to be more clear, what did exactly Mr. Padalovic say to Zjelko Klimenta before this shot took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Keljo, don't run. I'll kill you." Keljo said: "Come on. Don't joke." Those were the words uttered by Keljo and Padalovic. He said: "Don't joke with me." Keljo started running and Padalovic aimed and killed Keljo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As far as you know, did Keljo have any particular reason to start running?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because other prisoners said: "Here's Hazim. Hazim." Then Keljo started running so he would enter the hangar before Hazim Delic arrived. That was the reason why Keljo was running.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Dordic, did the Red Cross ever visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First some foreign team came. They introduced themselves as the Red Cross. They had cameras. Then after they left we were beaten. Some of us were given some statements saying how we were fine. Then when they left, we were beaten again. This was the first time when this foreign team came, and then the second time there was the International Red Cross. They had badges here on their chests (indicating) and it said "Red Cross". At that time we were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anything particular happen after this Red Cross visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the first team we were beaten. After the second team of the International Red Cross we were again beaten, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "the first team", do you mean that first team presented itself as Red Cross too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They presented themselves as Red Cross, but they did not anything -- any insignia with them. They had a video camera and they shot with this camera. There were four or five of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, when did you leave Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left -- I was transferred to the Musala sports hall in the hall in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember when or approximately when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was up there for about a month and a half in the sports hall in Musala before I was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean, do you not remember approximately when you moved from Celebici to Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. I don't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. When were you released from any kind of detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finally was released on 29th November 1992, before the New Year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Dordic, do you remember that you had an interview with an investigator of this Tribunal in November last year? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. In that interview you said something slightly different from today. You said that you saw Mucic --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That sounds very much like someone who is about to be cross-examined by counsel who has called the witness. I respectfully object to that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How do you bring that in?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I just want to know why he is -- there is a slight contradiction but I leave it to the cross-examination. So in this case my examination-in-chief is finished, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examinations and the order in which you wish to take them?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Can I have just one moment to consult with ... we are a little bit out of the loop after two weeks. (Pause). Your Honours, we have our order. First, will be counsel for Mr. Delic; second, counsel for Mr. Mucic; third, counsel for Mr. Landzo; and, fourth, counsel for Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I too was a little off my usual pattern. So we break now and come back at 11.45. (11.15 am) (Short break). (11.45 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please invite the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, just one little housekeeping matter. As the court will recall, Mr. Delic has a bad back and has been authorised to stand. He just wanted me to remind the court of that and also remind the court that sometimes he has a grimace on his face. It is because of pain. It has absolutely nothing to do with the Tribunal or anything else. Last time we were here I believe the Trial Chamber made some remark about the defendants and Mr. Delic just wanted to apologise to the Trial Chamber if you thought that he was being in any way disrespectful. It is not that at all. It is simply that he is in severe pain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Anything that makes a defendant comfortable will be done. Actually the remark in the Trial Chamber was on a specific occasion. It wasn't a general one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour, but Mr. Delic just wanted to ensure that the Trial Chamber understood that he has the greatest respect for the court as an institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will take care of what gives him pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (Witness re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Still remind him he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm reminding you that you are still under oath

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court? Good morning, Mr. Dordic. Mr. Dordic, my name is Tom Moran and I represent Hazim Delic in this case. I'm going to ask you some questions, mainly things about what you have already testified about. Sometimes I talk a little fast. Sometimes my questions aren't as clear as they ought to be. If I talk a little fast or if my question isn't clear, would you do me a favour and stop me and ask me to repeat it so that you understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Another thing is: will you listen to the question and just answer the question that I ask? Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if it requires just a "yes" or a "no", can you answer it with just a "yes" or a "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. One other thing, and you have been real good about it so far but let me remind you, because you have been fairly quiet while I have been talking to you. There's two ladies that are other here, one is over here and one is over there. They are what is called court reporters. They have to write down everything that anyone of us says. If they can't hear you, they can't write it down. They can't just write down a nod, so you have to answer out loud. Can we do that to make their lives a little easier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually what counsel is saying is that answers should be by words, not by actions. If you want to nod, if a nod means yes, say "yes". If it means no, say "no" instead of shaking your head. Put whatever answers you want to give in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. The first thing I would like to ask you is: who did you talk to about your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today only with Mr. Prosecutor here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you talk to -- before today, did you talk to anybody about the testimony you were going to give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No-one at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No-one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How about someone maybe with the Association of Detainees in Belgrade? Did you talk to anybody about what you were going to say to anyone from the Association?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you talk to anyone possibly about -- from a television station about what you were going to testify to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I once appeared on television briefly at a time when the trial was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and you talked to them about your testimony, about what you were going to testify to here, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I talked about not being afraid about giving testimony, that I had no fear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You have gave a written statement to someone from the Prosecutor's office, a man named McLeod, back in November of last year; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And have you given any other statements to anybody about what you were going to -- about your testimony or about what happened to you in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only to McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, as I recall, you testified on your direct examination that you were arrested on July 12th 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was on St Peter's Day. It was in July. So there was a confusion over the date. It wasn't June, but July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, but you remember it because it was St Peter's Day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You testified on direct that the morning after you were brought to Celebici Mr. Mucic, Pavo Mucic, came to you and your brother and your father and told your father that he was going to be released. Isn't that what you testified to on direct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the statement that you gave to Mr. McLeod? That's not what you said then, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did say the interpreter to tell Mr. McLeod. I don't know if he did interpret it that way in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about how the statement was taken; okay, just technically how it was taken. What would happen would be Mr. McLeod would say something in English, ask a question; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then the interpreter would interpret it to me into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, and the interpreter was -- well -- then you would answer into Serbian; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then the interpreter or somebody would type what you said in English; right? Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not the interpreter. The interpreter was interpreting to Mr. McLeod and Mr. McLeod was doing that in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then after -- he would write down what you said and then he would ask another question; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When it was all over, the interpreter read you the statement in Serbian; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you could make any corrections you wanted to on that statement, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And after the person -- after the interpreter read it to you and you had a chance to make any corrections you wanted, then you signed the bottom of each page and you signed the back, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I signed the statement that I gave to Mr. McLeod in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So after it was typed, the final version, that was read to you in Serbian before you signed anything; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask -- in the statement that you signed and that the interpreter from the Tribunal certified was a correct interpretation it says that your father -- you say: "My father was released on that morning and I heard later that others from Zukici were also released." Did you say that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Later they were all released together, the rest of the ones who were arrested on the 13th. They were released to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said in your statement: "He was taken from the hangar by a man who introduced himself as Delic. I later learned that his first name was Hazim". Did you say that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when Mr. McLeod and the interpreter wrote that down, they didn't put down what you said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I first saw Pavo Mucic that morning of 13th July when he introduced himself to my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Let me ask that question again. Maybe you didn't understand it. What I said was: when the interpreter and Mr. McLeod wrote that down, they didn't write down what you said; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Apparently the interpreter did not interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when the interpreter said that she is a duly qualified and approved by the Registry of the International Criminal Tribunal for prosecutions of persons responsible for serious violations of international law and that she interpreted for you and you understood what she interpreted, she was not telling the truth, was she?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object to this type of question to this witness. He couldn't say anything about the behaviour of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has just said that the interpreter did not fully and fairly interpret what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, isn't it sufficient to say that that was not what he told her?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, he has just said that the interpreter or Mr. McLeod wrote down something he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's in contradiction with what he is now saying, the matter is established, because going further doesn't even get you anywhere other than the fact that he is denying that he said that. That's all it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's true, your Honour. What he is saying is that the Office of the Prosecutor or the interpreter for the OTP misstated some things that he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. You understand what he says?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is what he means. Don't pursue it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Somewhere in your statement, the same paragraph, you said that you saw Mr. Delic several times walking around the camp and the way it reads here it says: "Delic walked normally and I never saw that he had a wounded leg." Did you tell that to the investigators from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I never noticed that he had any wound on his leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And he always walked normally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He always walked normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did someone ask you if he had a wounded leg or he walked normally, or did you just volunteer that when you made your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say it voluntarily. I got that question from Mr. McLeod, who asked and then this was later translated, interpreted into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you ever meet a man named Memic -- M-E-M-I-C I believe is how it is spelt -- while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Memic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes. Wasn't he the person that interrogated you at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor you said that you were interrogated -- the day you were interrogated was the first time you met Pavo Mucic; is that right? The first time you met Mr. Mucic was at the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I saw Mucic was on 13th July, when he came to the hangar and he told us that my late father, Jelenko Dordic, could go home, and that the two of us, Jelenko and myself, were staying in the camp to make a statement, and that he would let us go later too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So if your written statement to the Office of the Prosecutor says: "On my second full day in Celebici I met Pavo Mucic for the first time", that would be wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw Pavo Mucic and the second time was when I was giving the statement in the office near the registration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me read that full sentence. What your statement says is: "On my second full day in Celebici I met Pavo Mucic for the first time, when I was taken for interrogation, and he introduced himself to me and my brother as Pavo." That wasn't the first time you met him, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the second time that I saw Pavo Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that was about five or ten days after you were brought to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So when it says in your statement on your second full day in Celebici, " ... I met Pavo Mucic for the first time when I was taken for interrogation", that is another one of those things where the interpreter for the Office of the Prosecutor got it all wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You never said it to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I saw Pavo Mucic for the first time on the 13th and for the second time when I was giving the statement in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is right. When they said that you said -- that's a bad question. Let me start over. When someone from the Office of the Prosecutor, apparently Mr. McLeod, wrote down that you said in essence that you were interrogated on your second full day in Celebici, you met Pavo then and it was the first time, they got it all wrong; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I saw him on 13th July and a second time when I saw Pavo when I was giving my statement, five or ten days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. McLeod and the interpreter got it all wrong when they typed up your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is unnecessary. I think he has said everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, if I can have a moment, I think, believe it or not, I may be done. (Pause). Your Honour, I'm going to pass the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Dordic, I'm going to ask you some questions, please, to start off with, about your education, which you told us about earlier on this morning. I would just like to have some more details, please, if you'll help me about that. All right? Can you tell us precisely at what stage you started school, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, please, the name of the school to which you went? Do you remember that, please? That was in Konjic, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to elementary school in Bradina. It was called Vonimir Welz School.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You stayed at that school throughout your education, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You stayed there for a total of how many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent seven years in that school. I repeated one grade. The first grade I repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think in evidence this morning you said you were there for eight years. Are you quite sure about exactly how long you were there? Was it eight years or seven years, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Seven years I was in that school and I completed my 8th grade in Tarcin as a part-time student.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What was the name of that school in Tarcin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the name of the school in Tarcin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why did you go to Tarcin to finish off your education, Mr. Dordic? Was there any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no particular reason, but my late father, Jelenko, had friends there, and he helped me to finish 8th grade there, so that I wouldn't lag behind my generation, so that I could continue my education, so I passed my exams as a part-time student.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Had you been lagging behind in your education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I repeated one year, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you have any educational problems that caused you to lag or to have to repeat that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't good at maths.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You'd better join a fairly large club then, Mr. Dordic. I can't admit to being the greatest mathematician on earth. Tell me this then: you went to what my learned friend Mr. Turone describes as technical school. Can you just tell us what sort of course you did at that school after you'd left your elementary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed a course for firemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That took you two years, did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What sort of qualification did you get at the end of that course, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I acquired the qualification of a graduate of secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then you had a period as a construction worker. Was that because you couldn't get a job as a fireman anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for six months in a construction company called Granica in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You did your army service after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I went to another company, the railroads, Elbos -- the company is called Elbos -- and I went to do my military service from Elbos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That was for two years you did your army service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One year. One year, the military service. Before it was 18 months and then they reduced it to one year, to 12 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You had some initial training. Did you complete your initial training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed my initial training in Sviliniz as a baker.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were not being trained, for example, as an infantry man or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was there any particular reason why you weren't given basic military training, that you were simply trained as a baker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were mostly being trained in baking. We worked in the barracks and prepared as bakers for wartime circumstances within the grounds of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After your military service you then went back to the railway for a while; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What were your duties as a fireman? What sort of job did you do as a fireman, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a fireman I registered incoming trucks and I was the leader of the shift which consisted of five men.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I would like now to ask you, please, about an organisation which is responsible for Serbian refugees. Can you help us about this: you appeared on this television programme, Mr. Dordic. How did you come to be contacted by the television station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to Belgrade to look for relief, for assistance, because I didn't have any clothes to wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: When was that, Mr. Dordic, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe a month and a half or a month ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So in May of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And who was it that you approached for help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked them for help. It wasn't they who asked me for anything. It was the other way round.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That wasn't quite the question I asked you. I don't want to be difficult, but just tell us who it was you actually spoke to and discussed getting help with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up there the people responsible, there is the Konjic Detainees' Association. They founded their own association to help people who had fled over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And, what, you went simply to their offices, did you, when you went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned where their offices were from my friends and they told me that they had helped them to get some clothes and to get something to live off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So you went to the offices and you spoke, what, to a receptionist or a secretary, did you, when you went in first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke to the doorman, asked him where the offices were. Then I went up to the offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Had you had any contact at all with this organisation prior to this visit that you made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So let's just go through it. You were sent upstairs by the doorman. Then you went into the offices themselves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who did you speak to in the offices, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time I met Dusitsa Bojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What did you talk about with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I needed help.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did she want to know who you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later through my story she learned who I was, where I had been and then she helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you tell her that you were due to be a witness at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She knew I was in Belgrade to make the statement for Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So she already knew of your existence as a witness prior to your arriving at their offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did she tell you how she knew about that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you give any sort of statement to the Serbian Refugees' Organisation whilst you were there, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not make any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you talk about your evidence that you were going to give to this Tribunal? Did you talk about that at all with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That wasn't quite the question I asked, was it, Mr. Dordic? Did you discuss your evidence with her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How did you get in touch with the television station? Whose idea was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I happened to be there by chance. The day I came there to ask for relief, it was just by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Who asked you if you would give an interview to the television people? Whose idea was it, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked me whether I would be willing to talk and I said there would be no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, was it the people from the organisation who asked you to give an interview or the people from the television station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people from the television station.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment, please? (Pause). Who else at the Association did you meet on that occasion, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were lots of people in the office. I saw them for the first time, so I don't know who they were, nor what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you join the organisation as a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later, at the time I became a member of the Association. I said I needed help because there was nothing I could really do. I had to find a way of living.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did they say that you had to join the organisation before you could get any help? Is that what it came to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have you been to their offices on subsequent occasions and met with people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Have they been in touch with you? Have they contacted you since your visit there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any contact with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So let's just summarise this: you made one single visit to their offices. You have joined the organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: By sheer coincidence there just happened to be a TV crew visiting on that very day that you happened to be there; that's what it comes to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. You've been asked, Mr. Dordic, about your evidence concerning the first evening which you spent in the camp at Celebici. I want just to get it quite clear the process by which you came to give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. Did that take just a single day for it to be recorded, what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Belgrade or when Mr. McLeod came?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help me about this: you have made a statement to somebody in Belgrade, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any statements in Belgrade anywhere, only with Mr. McLeod, when I gave the statement to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help me, Mr. Dordic: why did you need me to clarify to you whether I meant in Belgrade or Mr. McLeod, if you haven't made a statement to somebody in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember giving anybody else a statement in Belgrade. I just made a statement to Mr. McLeod when they looked me up on the telephone. The police looked for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, but a moment or two ago when I asked you how long it took for your statement to be recorded your reply was: "In Belgrade or when Mr. McLeod came?" Why did you mention "in Belgrade", if you have not made a statement, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no other except that statement for Mr. McLeod. That was the first time I came in December, when Mr. McLeod came to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So why would it be necessary for you, when asked the question, to say and ask me to clarify it: "In Belgrade or Mr. McLeod" if you haven't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Frankly, if he said he made no statement in Belgrade, I don't see what you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would your Honour just give me a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is not being fair when you repeatedly ask the questions. You asked him the third time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So you were seen by Mr. McLeod. How long did it take to record your statement, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made the statement in the morning from 8 o'clock in the morning until somewhere around 7 o'clock in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At the end of the day you were taken through all of the writing that had been put down; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a man who was interpreting. I don't recall exactly his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So the man who was interpreting had the document in front of him which had been dictated by you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And at the end of that procedure did you sign each page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed in Latin script and with my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And can I just remind you of doing this: you also signed a certificate at the end of the statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You remember that being read over to you and you signing it and dating it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a certificate and I remember signing it as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept from me that it reads in part: "This statement has been read over to me in the Serbian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And what you had told Mr. McLeod that day, that was the truth, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you also, when having the statement read over to you by the interpreter, the gentleman who was interpreting on behalf of the OTP, acknowledge to the interpreter that the facts and matters that had been read over to you, as translated by that person, were true to the best of your knowledge and recollection? Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is that because what had been read out to you was true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you just explain what you mean by "partially", please, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So it was fully correct or only partially correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is like buying a pig in a poke. He doesn't even know what those statements are now, except to the extent to which he recollects.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We'll see whether we can just take it a little further and clarify it, if we may; for your Honours' assistance, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, because unless he knows what he said then, then he will not know whether it is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was going to come to that, if I may. You have been asked about your account concerning Mr. Mucic and the first night when you were at the camp, Mr. Dordic. Do you accept that what you have said in evidence and what you signed as being correct in your statement are two quite different things concerning that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Pavo Mucic for the first time when I was taken to the camp, the second day after I came to the camp, and when I was giving my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you understand that the statement which you gave to the Office of the Prosecution and the evidence which you have given are two quite different things? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Let me just put it to you another way, Mr. Dordic.
