Will you accept from me that the evidence you have given about Mr. Mucic that night, that's evidence you told us about this morning, is completely different from what you recorded to Mr. McLeod and the interpreter in November of last year? Will you accept that from me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made a statement first to McLeod. He asked me questions. I do not know how the interpreter translated what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But you've told us it was read over to you at the end, so you had an opportunity to clarify it, to change it in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For changing the statement I didn't have time, because the translator read it out to me fast. He was reading it fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, what I suggest to you, Mr. Dordic, is that it's not true that Mr. Mucic came to see you that first night. That's why it's not in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Asked and answered. Everything in Mr. Moran's cross-examination. Anyway, we do not object if Mr. Greaves wants to enter into evidence the previous statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He is entitled to ask his own questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm grateful. One occasionally likes to put a slightly different slant on matters from one's esteemed colleagues. The question was, Mr. Dordic: I suggest to you that it's not true that Mr. Mucic saw you in the way you have described on your first night in the camp, and that is why it's not in your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod didn't ask me that. He asked me when I was arrested and I answered. They didn't put that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help me about this, please, Mr. Dordic: when you told Mr. McLeod that it wasn't until you were interrogated by Mr. Mucic, that was the first time that you met him, that was also incorrect, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not correct. The first time I saw him was when he came to Number 6 on 13th July. He took me, my brother and my late father out from Number 6 and he said: "Jelenko, you're going home and your two sons are staying here to make a statement, and they'll follow you shortly." That was the first time I saw Pavo Mucic. He introduced himself to my father. He shook hands with him and he said he was Pavo Mucic. The second time was when I was giving the statement in the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help us about this, and perhaps you might like to stand up and point to it: which building do you say that this interrogation took place in, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the command building near the entrance gate. That was how they called it, this building, at the reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you see the big scale plan that's in front of us, the model? Just point it out on there, please, Mr. Dordic. Point out the building that you say you were interrogated in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please let us tell the witness if he wants to walk around and watch, of course, comfortably the model he can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I will of course do that. Mr. Dordic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are free to go out and be as close as possible to the building you can identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You may need to be careful with your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I believe he has never seen before this model.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Which is the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For the purposes of the written record, it's the building that is coloured red. Thank you very much, Mr. Dordic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can go back to your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On which side of the building do you say the room was where you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you need to get up and point again -- is it on my side of the building or, as it were, the railway side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On your side, that side, at the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And we can see that there are some rooms with windows that go down nearly to the ground and then some windows that are about two-thirds of the way up the wall. Were you interrogated in the ones with the windows two-thirds of the way up the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was questioned and the window was facing the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So that we're clear again, would you like just to take the pointer, please, again, and just tell us which building you think of as the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Indicating) this is where the infirmary was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just for the sake -- thank you very much, Mr. Dordic. You can sit down again, if you like, please. Just for the sake of clarity, that's a building that's on, as it were, the side of the main part of the camp. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Not on my side of the model.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Near the building parallel to where I was questioned; across from that building was the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In your evidence this morning you spoke about Hazim Delic using a pistol in some way. Can you explain to us, please, why in the statement which you made to Mr. McLeod there is no mention whatever of such an incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned -- I don't know if the interpreter said that, but I mentioned all the details that I knew when I was giving this statement. I said everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But someone waving a pistol around and using it on you, that's a fairly significant item of information, isn't it? Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic personally forced me to sign this statement, but I was not saying anything. He was dictating it to Ismeta and Ismeta was typing it up. Then he forced me to sign it. I wanted to sign it in the Roman alphabet, but I had to do it in the Cyrillic alphabet there in that administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, what I want to suggest to you, Mr. Dordic, is that your account that you have given us of that interrogation today was quite different from what you put down and signed as being true in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object to that. It's not so different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No mention of an incident with a pistol, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that to the interpreter that he was holding it here against my temple (indicating), and then he hit me at the top of my head, and at that time he also slapped me, and then he took me to the toilet to wash up, because my nose was bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you are not telling the truth about that incident, Mr. Dordic. That's why that matter that you've just recounted isn't in your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that in Belgrade. I don't know -- I don't know if this interpreter did interpret this to Mr. McLeod, because he asked me everything from when I was first arrested and how I was giving the statement and I responded to all the questions in Belgrade and I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a man called Ivica Buric, please. Was that someone you knew at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him at all, because I worked in Sarajevo, and in Konjic I did not work ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Buric at the camp in Celebici whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, because a long time has gone by.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I refresh your memory, please, with what you told Mr. McLeod in your statement to the OTP about him, and see if that refreshes your memory: "I know Ivica Buric", it says. "He worked at the camp. He occasionally came to the hangar with Delic." Then you describe how Mr. Buric would beat people, but less frequently than other people. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You obviously lost members of your family as a result of the war, Mr. Dordic, and I'm very sympathetic towards you concerning that. I hope you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lost my father, my mother, my aunt -- two aunts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Has that made you very bitter towards the people that had got you incarcerated at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At one point I was thinking when I heard that my father and my mother and two aunts were killed -- I was wondering why I was not with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it also because you weren't there to protect them, Mr. Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean to protect my father and mother?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, because you were locked up at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I was forcibly detained there without a reason because I had no weapons issued to me, and I belonged to no organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't want to distress you in any way, Mr. Dordic. I hope you understand that. I just want to explore this a little way, please. Did you feel guilty at not being able to protect your family because you were detained at Celebici? Is that one of the things that made you feel bitter towards the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At one point I thought that it would have been better if they had released me on 13th July, so we would all be killed together, rather than go through all the tortures I suffered at Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Dordic. What I want to ask you is this: do you see the people working at Celebici camp whilst you were there as being in some way responsible for the deaths of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I could stay in prison, why my late father could not stay there? There was no reason for him to be detained. He also was not issued any weapons. So I could have been released with them when they were released, both myself and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you go so far as to say that you hate the people who kept you detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that I hated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But you are very bitter about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm advised that we have a dead computer over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It is no longer recording the transcript, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If we can get the engineer to see what is wrong. We will find someone to come and look at it. (Pause.) Mr. Ackerman, I think we might rise now and come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. (12.50 pm) (Luncheon Adjournment) 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly invite the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May I bring something to the court's attention before the witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a result of some of the testimony this morning I'm becoming, and I think I share this with several of my colleagues, increasingly concerned about the issue of whether or not these witnesses have made statements other than statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and, if so, where they are. If we start first with the witness that was on the stand today, your Honours will remember that there was a time when he was asked by Mr. Greaves about his statement and the witness said: "In Belgrade or the one to Mr. McLeod?", giving some of us at that point the impression that he was identifying that he had made more than one statement with regard to what happened to him in this case. The evidence for that continues to mount. Your Honours will remember the videotape that this witness appeared on that we played for you and gave you a transcript of, where there was much talk in the nature of "our witnesses", in the nature of "how we have prepared them well", and things like that. We also have, and I will make these a part of the record as soon as I can, a newspaper clipping from a newspaper called Telegraf, which is a Serbian weekly of March 6th, 1996, where one of the witnesses that the prosecution is going to be calling this week told the reporter that: "All the statements given by witnesses to the Association of Detainees are translated into English and signed by the witnesses. All those statements are to be forwarded to the legal counsel of the Tribunal group, Teresa McHenry, who investigates the Muslim crimes against the Serbs." Now I don't know whether those statements were, in fact, forwarded to her or not, but that is certainly evidence that the statements exist. Then just recently there has been -- there is apparently an internal battle going on inside the Association of Detainees in Belgrade in which the President is being accused by other functionaries in that Association of doing some things that are improper. The President gave an interview -- and his name is Petar Fiodorov -- President of the Association of Detainees gave an interview to a newspaper called Gradjanin, which was published on June 17, 1997, in which he said some very interesting things. He said: "To become a member of that Association", as this witness indicated that he was, "a pre-condition for getting a membership card was to give a statement". He claims that that is blackmail, because the only way you could get help from this Association, that this witness indicated he was asking for, is to give such a statement. The President of the Association calls that blackmail. He says elsewhere in connection with his interview that: "The statements of the detainees were placed at places used to make coffee." He is complaining that they were just left lying around the office, but that certainly is evidence that there are such statements and that those statements exist. The next thing that is of concern is the connection between the Association of Detainees and the Serbian government in Belgrade, headed by Slobodan Milosevic. This President again says: "The commission that was working on the Celebici case, which was led by Dusitsa and Branka, was financed by different ministries", leaving the impression at least that those were ministries of the Serbian government, and this Association of Detainees, although referred to as an NGO, is simply a shadow organisation of the Serbian government. It seems to me that there may be more fire than smoke with regard to this issue at this point, and that something needs to be done to finally and totally clarify this. I would propose several things. First of all, let me say it would be a terrible thing to happen to this Tribunal if this Tribunal is being used by the Serbian government as an extension of what went on during the war in some way. This Association seems to be very anxious in assisting the Tribunal in prosecuting Muslims and providing information against Muslims but certainly it has not been very anxious to send its war criminals to this Tribunal. One wonders about that. I would propose the following: first of all, that the prosecution state for the record whether or not they have any statements that were received from the Association of Detainees that were made by these witnesses, signed and translated into English, as one of these witnesses apparently told a newspaper reporter; if they don't have them, state whether or not they know of their existence and whether or not such statements, in fact, exist; third of all, that the prosecution be asked without delay to investigate the source of all this information that such statements exist and determine whether or not, in fact, they do, and if they do, make them available; finally, that the prosecution look into the connection, if any, between this Association of Detainees and Slobodan Milosevic's government in Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't know how far the trial of this Trial Chamber can be diverted. I suppose if every information which comes out of newspapers or gossips are followed, there will be no end to this trial. There are statutory provisions enabling you to ask from the prosecution whatever statements they have and they should offer you all the statements within their possession. If you don't have more than that and you know further statements, I suppose you might be able to procure them and confront them with it, but I do not think we could go on a wild goose chase for every statement which comes out in newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand, your Honours, that I am not asking for any kind of a delay, not even a five-minute delay. I am prepared to go forward with this witness and all other witnesses, but these are matters which are of grave concern to us and they just keep coming up time after time after time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: From what I observe, it's likely to come up until it is finished because there has been every occasion for anybody to bring in their fashion of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I don't know if your Honours want me to speak to this at all. I certainly agree with your Honours that the fact that something may or may not be said in the press is not evidence, and defence counsel has been given extremely wide latitude to cross-examine the witnesses about their ties with the Association, and they are, of course, free to do what they want. I will state for the record that if the prosecution has statements of these witnesses, they have been provided to the defence. I don't know that the prosecution would take the position that in all circumstances if they are not Office of the Prosecutor statements, we need to, but, in fact, in this case if we have a statement from one of the witnesses that is at all related to Celebici, that has been provided. With respect to the issue about what was in the paper, I believe that this was clarified at one of the prior hearings, when defence counsel raised this -- brought this matter up, which is that it appears that the statement about what was being done and what was translated into English has to do with a mission in Timosoira that the Association arranged many of the logistics for, because the Office of the Prosecutor was not permitted to enter the FRY. The Association arranged the logistics, and the Tribunal investigators interviewed people in Timosoira. Those statements are translated as the witness speaks into English and then were brought back to The Hague. The Association does not have copies of those statements. That is what at least the prosecution believes is the most likely explanation for what was in the paper. As to whether or not there are additional statements that witnesses have given or have not given, other than to say that we don't have any specific information, they are not in our possession, and their existence, to the extent such statements exist, there is certainly nothing improper about them. People are entitled to give statements about what happened to them to whomever they want, and as to whether or not the idea the prosecution should look into the funding of this, regardless of who funds this Association, the prosecution doesn't believe that is relevant in the absence of any evidence that the Association has done anything improper to subvert the course of justice here. If the defence themselves wants to do some of their own investigation because they disagree with us and think that it is relevant, of course they are able to, but we don't believe that it's the least bit relevant. NGOs and governments often have biases or whatever on one side or the other and often help, but that's not necessarily a reason to find what they are doing is improper. The issue is: have they done anything to improperly influence the witnesses in this case? I believe this has been examined at great length and the prosecution believe there is absolutely no evidence to suggest that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the impression that is being given by the series of newspaper articles is this -- it is probably deliberate on the part of the Serbian government organisations, but I know that -- but the impression that is being given is that the Office of the Prosecution is the cat's paw of the Serbian government. If that is the impression going abroad, then it is one that the prosecution ought, in my respectful submission, to consider very seriously, because for them to be seen by the outside world as in any way associated with one particular side of this conflict would fatally undermine the authority of this Tribunal. With the greatest respect to my learned friend Mr.s McHenry, for her to be dismissive about this problem is in my respectful submission unwise on her part. The prosecution as a whole must start to address this problem, because the impression that is being given when the Serbian Refugees' Organisation talks of "our witnesses" is that this Tribunal is no more than an arm of the Serbian political establishment. That's a very dangerous and subversive thing to be getting abroad, and it is one which, in my respectful submission, lies at the heart of the complaint that we have and the concerns we have, because we are interested not just in our clients' cases but also interested that this should be a just -- and seen to be a just proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell the witness to come? (Witness re-enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you please remind him he is on his oath?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still testifying under oath?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: May it please the court. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Dordic, my name is John Ackerman. I'm one of the lawyers representing Esad Landzo in this case. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions I want to ask you. If I ask you a question that you do not understand, please give me an opportunity to re-ask it so that you can understand it; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not getting a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you have some confusion about one of my questions, don't assume you understand without letting me know and maybe I can rephrase it in a way that you will understand it; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Some time ago previous to your appearance in this court you had in some manner instructed the prosecution to request protection for your appearance here; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew, did you not, that this court had entered an order granting you that protection? You knew that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you knew that that meant that your name and address and identifying data about you was to be kept secret and not revealed to the public in any way for your protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now with that all in mind and knowing that all those efforts have been made by everyone here, including the court, you appeared on Belgrade TV on May 27, 1997 under your own name; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told them who you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your name appeared on the screen of that programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you talked about the things you claim had happened to you at Celebici camp in that programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told Mr. Greaves this morning, when he was questioning you, that the reason you gave that interview was that you were asked to do so by the Belgrade TV station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So someone must have given them your name and identified for them knowledge that you had for them to be interested in talking to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you run up to them when you saw the cameras there, saying, you know: "My name is Vaso Dordic. I know about Celebici. Please interview me. I want to be on TV." Is that the way it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The way it happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just happened to be there. I came to ask for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How did they know that you were somebody that they might be interested in interviewing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was talking to the Association they were there. I don't know why they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you were talking to the Association about your need for clothing; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was saying that I needed clothing, that I needed accommodation and some aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were not interested in interviewing you about your need for clothing, accommodation and aid, though, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were interested in interviewing you about your experiences in Celebici; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know how they knew that I was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Someone must have told them; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, surely. I don't know how they learned my real name. They -- some people sent me to the Association to seek assistance. I went to Belgrade. I sought assistance from them, asking them to give me clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there was someone there at the Association who knew who you were and knew about your experiences in Celebici apparently; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody knew. That was the first time I saw Mr.s Dusitsa Bojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the television people just sort of made a lucky guess that you might know something about Celebici?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw Dusitsa Bojic, when I came to ask for assistance. A TV crew was there. I introduced myself to Mr.s Dusitsa Bojic. I told her who I was, where I came from, where I'd been, and that I needed assistance badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was the TV crew permitted to overhear the conversation you had with Ms. Bojic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. How do I know? They were there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you talked to Ms. Bojic, was it in an office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the TV crew was in the office while you were talking to Ms. Bojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you mentioned to Ms. Bojic that your name was Vaso Dordic, and that you had been a detainee in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And knowing that you had asked for and been granted protection by this court, you agreed to give up all that protection and go on television in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't give up the protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the protection was designed to keep your name and the circumstances of what happened to you at Celebici secret and private and not disclosed to the public, wasn't it? Isn't that what the protection was designed for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you go on television that goes on satellite all over Europe, that kind of gives that up, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How did I know that that would go on television?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if there's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know at all it would go on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you sat in front of TV cameras with an interviewer asking you questions and giving answers to those questions with no idea that this would be broadcast on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you told by them that they would not use it, that they would keep it secret?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't say anything. They simply approached me and started to interview me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you told by Ms. Bojic that it would be kept secret and it would be no problem for you to talk with them, because they wouldn't reveal anything? Did she tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. She didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you just assumed that you could give an interview to a commercial public television station and that they would respect your privacy and not broadcast it? Is that what you are telling the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you have talked now with Belgrade TV about this situation; you have talked with Mr. McLeod about this situation; you have talked with Mr. Turone about this situation, your testimony. Who else have you talked to about your experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only with Mr. McLeod and the gentleman when I came here, with no-one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if that's the case, how did Mr. McLeod know to talk to you? How did he even know who you were?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The witness could even not know how investigators can reach his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how Mr. McLeod would have had any idea that you were of interest in this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know at all how they found out my name, that I had come out of prison and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because before Mr. McLeod approached you, you had never told anyone else that you had been a prisoner at Celebici; is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is his answer not conclusive that he did not know? I thought it was conclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine with me, your Honour. That's fine with me. So the first time you spoke of what happened to you in Celebici was to Mr. McLeod on November 15, 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first time that I was giving a statement to Mr. McLeod in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that wasn't my question. My question was: that was the first time you had spoken with anyone about your experiences in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now was there any reason, after having asked the prosecution to secure protection for you, and after having put this court through the process of considering the matter and issuing you an order giving you that protection, based upon your fear, that you would then go on television and say on television: "I'm not afraid at all"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That one is not asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him tell us why he did not want protection any longer. That's what he's asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What made you decide on that day in May 1997 to give up that protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not give up the protection. They were just telling me this interview and I gave them this interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you didn't ask them that your name be protected or that your face be blurred or anything like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How did I know that I would be on television? I just didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see yourself on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you seen the tape since then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what you said on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now that was in May of 1997, about two months ago; correct? Less than two months ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't remember when you gave the interview to Belgrade television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that it was this year but I don't remember the month and the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have testified at length here today about things that happened in 1992, five years ago, and now you're telling us you can't remember what happened in 1997, when you talked to Belgrade TV, and what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall all exact details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you testified to a lot of exact details about what you claim happened to you in Celebici five years ago, yet you don't remember any exact details about your television interview two months ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony this morning you told this court several dates, the date that Bradina was first attacked, the date that Bradina was second attacked, the date that you were arrested in your home, the date that you went to Celebici camp, the date that your father was released from Celebici camp, the date that you were released from Celebici camp. You can remember all those dates, but you can't remember what date you were interviewed by Belgrade TV two months ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know which television this was, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that the reason you can tell this court about things that you claim happened to you in Celebici camp was because someone else told you all those things and you had memorised all those things, so that you could come here today and say them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody -- in fact, I did not have any contact with anyone here before this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now on November 15th 1996 you were interviewed by Mr. McLeod; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of my colleagues has just handed me a note and let me just take a moment and ask you this question: have you been interviewed by other television stations other than the one that we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no other television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: He says he didn't even know he would be on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what prompted the question whether there might be multiple interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There might be many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to November 15th 1996 when you were interviewed by Mr. McLeod. Do you remember that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was in 1996, but what month and date, that I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you don't know whether it was February, April, November, October? You don't know what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the dates. The month I do know. I know that it was December 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: December of 1996 was when he interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That interview took place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the building in New Belgrade, in the offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that the offices of the Association of Detainees or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. It wasn't the Association of Detainees at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was the organisation that that office belonged to; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The international offices. Down there -- I gave the interview down there to Mr. -- I mean the statement -- to Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us this morning that this was an interview process that lasted from 8.00 in the morning until 7.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 11 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in that seven (sic) hours, what was produced out of that seven hours was a seven-page statement. At least that's what I have, a seven-page statement. Are you aware of that, that that's all that came out of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There must have been a lot of things said back and forth between you and Mr. McLeod that didn't make it into this statement, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if all the details came in, but I spent 11 hours with Mr. McLeod in Belgrade. That was when I first gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that 11 hours he was asking questions and you were giving him answers; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was asking questions and I was giving answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now you have been testifying here today for maybe two and a half hours total, and in that amount of time we've produced 93 pages of transcript; does that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. The witness has no control on how a record is typed by other persons during his interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's my point. That's exactly my point. Thank you, Mr. Turone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The person typing was a novice or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The person typing was not the witness anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is exactly what he wants to know. Two and a half hours produced 93 pages and 11 hours produced only 7 pages. Maybe something which he said was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it 11 continuous hours of questioning or did you have breaks within that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I entered into the building at 8 o'clock in the morning and I left the building at 7 o'clock at night, and I had an hour break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there were only ten hours of questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things that you knew on that date that you gave this statement to Mr. McLeod was you knew that Mr. Landzo had been arrested and was in custody of the International Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When I was giving that statement, that is when Mr. McLeod told me about that. Until that time I didn't know about it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. He told you that. He also told you that Mr. Delic, Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic had also been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so in the course of that discussion with Mr. McLeod you learned that the four people from Celebici, who had been arrested, were in custody and going to be tried, were the four that are in this courtroom today: Mr. Landzo, Delic, Mucic and Delalic; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know they were going to be tried.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You heard they had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard they had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What Mr. McLeod told you they were interested in was anything you could do to help gather evidence against these four defendants; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod said that I should give a statement to him how I experienced my sufferings in the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you knew that these were the four people who had been arrested and the four people who he was interested in your talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew that other people had not been arrested. You knew that Padalovic had not been arrested, or you were not told that he had been; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And Osman Dedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a guard called Makaron?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. And there were some others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew things about what all these other people had done at Celebici and all these other guards had done, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course, because of the bitterness that you told Mr. Greaves about this morning, you were very anxious at that point to help Mr. McLeod as much as you possibly could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, there came a time, did there not, when you were asked if you would be willing to speak to representatives of these defendants, and you refused to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not refuse anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall very well that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall anyone from the prosecution telling you that representatives of the defendants in this case wanted to talk with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So at least to the extent that representation might have been made to this court it didn't apply to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you gave that statement to Mr. McLeod in Belgrade in December of 1996, he told you that he -- the Office of the Prosecutor had interviewed Mr. Landzo, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And he told you things that Mr. Landzo had said during the course of that interview, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He told you, didn't he, that Mr. Landzo had said during his interview that he had an injured hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me while Landzo Zenga was hitting me whether he had a bandaged hand and I said that he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the question was whether his hand had a bandage on it and not whether or not you noticed that it was injured; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see a bandage on his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when your statement claims that you said that Mr. Landzo did not have an injured hand, that wouldn't be true; what you really said was that you didn't see a bandage on his hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him in the Celebici camp with a bandage on his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. Do you know today, as you sit here, whether or not Mr. Landzo has an injury to his hand and had an injury to his hand without a bandage on it during the time he was at Celebici and today? Do you know that? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now you have told us today that you were arrested at Zukici on 12th July 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 12th, on St Peter's Day. That was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were brought to Celebici, along with several other persons; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not other people. It was my mother, father, brother, aunts and a relative and two of their children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: First you went to a hotel in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Between the time you were arrested and the time you got to the motel in Konjic, you were beaten, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were beaten in the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was beaten in the motel besides you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Beside me, my brother was beaten up in the motel, Savo Dordic, my late father, my late mother, Radojka Dordic and Gosa Dordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who it was beat you at the Konjic motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were some men there and there was a young woman there and they called her Gara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were these people wearing uniforms or did they appear to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had uniforms on, camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And any insignia on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some did; some did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The one or more who beat you, did any of those have insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The insignias were TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the judges in as much detail as you can possibly remember the injuries that you received during these beatings at the motel in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They kicked us and they beat us with hands and with rifles and other things. Savo Dordic had part of his ear cut off. They climbed onto the vehicle and cut off half of his ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was that that had his ear cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What specific injuries did you receive as a result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was kicked and I was hit in the back. I fell to the floor and they were also kicking me there over my back and also with the rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you become unconscious as a result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I even -- there was a soldier, one of them, and he even forced me to lick a wound that he had. So I had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any wounds? Were you bleeding as a result of these beatings at the Konjic motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not have any injuries on my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we had seen you after those beatings, would we have been able to tell that you had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you had marks on you at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the ones that are the consequences of my stay in Number 6 and also my teeth are broken. Until then I had all teeth in my upper jaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your teeth were broken during your beating at the Konjic motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was in Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Konjic motel. If we had been able to look at you after you were beaten at the Konjic motel, would we be able to tell that you'd been beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, of course, all of your relatives who were arrested with you on 12th July 1992 were the same ethnic background as you. All of you were Serbian; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so those who were released the next day, 13th July 1992, the people who released them knew that it was Serbian ethnic people that were being released from Celebici, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now give me your best approximation of when it was you were released from Celebici and sent to Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in 1992. I was altogether five months in prison. A month and a half of that I spent at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if you went to the prison middle of July, your position is then that you stayed there until middle of October, middle of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall saying in your statement to Mr. McLeod that you left Celebici at the end of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Middle of October or end of October. I don't know exactly the date. I spent a month and a half at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked a little bit ago about seeing the uniforms with the TO insignia on them. What does that insignia look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were circles and it had "TO" inside the circle. It was written in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. You told us this morning that Mr. Landzo beat you every day that you were at Celebici. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember also saying in your statement that after the visit of the Red Cross that there were several days that nobody was beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After the humanitarian organisation who came there the second time, there were several days that nobody was beaten, and then again they started beating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you say that Mr. Landzo beat you every day, that's a bit of an exaggeration, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not exactly every day. Sometimes every other day; every third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, knowing that Mr. McLeod was interested in Mr. Landzo, Mr. Delic, Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic, and because of your bitterness and your willingness to help the prosecution as much as possible, what actually happened was, because Padalovic and Osman Dedic and Makaron and several of these other guards who did things at Celebici were not arrested, you sort of made Esad Landzo the composite character of all these guards, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say that Esad Landzo was guilty for all the guards. They should have been arrested too. If he was arrested, then all of them should have been arrested too. I did not say that Esad Landzo is the only guilty one among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You took things that these other guards did to you and to other prisoners and blamed them on Mr. Landzo in the course of your statement to Mr. McLeod, because he was the only one under arrest; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the others beat too, not only Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For instance, the person who really forced you and your brother to do the sex incident that you testified about here this morning was not Mr. Landzo but Osman Dedic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true. Esad Landzo entered the Number 6 and he ordered us to take off our clothes and kneel down in front of one another, and he forced me to put my brother's sexual organ in my mouth and did that several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have already testified about that. My question was: "Wasn't it Osman Dedic that did that?", and I guess your answer is: "No, it was Mr. Landzo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Will you concede that Osman Dedic was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Osman Dedic was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Will you concede that Padalovic was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Padalovic was there, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right next to Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of the time that you were there, did you ever visit the command building other than the one time when you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the dispensary, because I was beaten up before that and my nose was bleeding, and it had all covered my face and my neck, and my brother and I went to the dispensary. Otherwise I didn't go there, to the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt you. Who gave you permission to go to the dispensary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic asked in the morning whether anybody needed to go. The two of us didn't dare apply and then he addressed the two of us and told us to go to the dispensary, because he saw that we were covered in blood, and he took us to the dispensary for them to clean us up, and then my brother's arm was also bandaged, because it had been broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you went to the dispensary one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You went to the command building one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you spend any time during the time you were there other than coming in and going out at the front gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Landzo was, I think you characterised in your statement, just an ordinary guard at Celebici; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that during the time you were there family members were permitted to bring food to prisoners on occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you were transferred to Musala, you saw Mr. Landzo there wearing a white belt, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed that he was then transferred to the military police, because he had a white belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the first day that you recall seeing Mr. Landzo at Musala wearing a white belt? When would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the day. Soon after I went to Musala, maybe ten or twenty days later was when I saw him wearing this white belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me now take you back to your testimony this morning about the shooting incident that you claim to have observed with Zeljko Klimenta. You remember that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now what you told us this morning was that you and Zeljko had gone outside together and that when this incident happened, you were standing by the front door of Hangar 6 and had not yet gone back inside, and that's how you were able to observe what happened. That's what you said this morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall telling Mr. McLeod in your interview with him in December in Belgrade that you were lying inside Hangar 6 when you saw this incident happen? Do you recall telling him that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was standing with Zeljko Klimenta, because that morning we had taken the bucket out. The bucket was at the bottom of the hangar which we used for toilet purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that was your testimony this morning. This must be another one of those instances where the translator that was present during your statement to Mr. McLeod did not understand the difference between standing outside and lying inside and therefore got it wrong; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he made a mistake in interpreting to Mr. McLeod. I said I was standing outside, outside the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what you said in your interview in Belgrade, wasn't it, that you were standing outside, just like you said here today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when the translator translated that as lying inside the hangar, that was a pretty lousy job of translation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have reason to believe that Padalovic shot Zeljko Klimenta on purpose, or do you tend to believe that that was an accident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was on purpose or whether it was an accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Padalovic distraught and crying after it had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he killed the late Zeljko Klimenta, Padalovic ran up. The other guards ran up too and closed the door, so I couldn't see at that moment whether Padalovic was crying, because the doors of Number 6 were closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that he was crying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again after that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some time I saw Padalovic again at the same spot, when we used to go to the toilet in the morning to urinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not he continued to work as a guard at Celebici after this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him after some time. After that I didn't see him. I was transferred to the sports centre at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now just to make certain that we're all clear about this, it's your testimony that this shooting happened in October, very shortly before you were taken to Musala; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us this morning that you became a member of some association in Belgrade. Which association was it you became a member of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an association of detainees from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what was it you had to do to become a member of that association?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you issued some kind of a membership card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a membership card.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think I could go there and become a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably. How do I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't know that -- in other words, you don't have to be a detainee to be a member, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are mostly people who were in camps that were members.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did they ask you, when you asked to be a member, if you'd been in a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you went there asking for help and they just said: "You have to be a member", and they didn't really care whether you'd been a detainee or not; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So maybe any of us in here could just walk in there and say: "I need clothes", and they would give us clothes without asking us anything. They would give us a membership card and give us clothes; right? Is that the way it works?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I object, your Honour. This is amounting to harassment. This witness has already stated how he became a member, how he spoke to the lady there in the Association and that the lady knew who he was, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm through with all those questions in any event, judge. I have another, however. Do you have your membership card with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it here in The Hague or is it back home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: White paper, cardboard paper. It's about this size (indicating) and it has my picture on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I assume it also has your name on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my name, first and last.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date of birth, where I was born and the municipality I was born in, which municipality I was born in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Does it also say the camp in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where did you get the picture for the card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had my photo taken for this card. I had my photo taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Somewhere other than the office of the Association?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't at all in the office of the Association. Outside at a photographer's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you came and asked to be a member, they told you that you had to go and get your photograph taken; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you still pursuing this trend, because I don't know what it's all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I think I'm through with that trend, although it continues to bother me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because he has admitted he is a member of the Association. There's no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. I'm concerned about what the President of the Association has said, that you cannot be a member if you don't give them a statement about your experiences, and I might ask you, Mr. Witness, if you were told that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That disqualifies you from being a member.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That disqualifies counsel from being a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that's true, I would be disqualified. Frankly I don't mind being disqualified. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Maybe you make a large donation and they will make you a member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's the last cross-examination. Do you have anything for him? I didn't see he had anything for your client, but if you still want to. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honour, you just said that this was the last cross-examination, because I don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Before his release, there's a matter that came up and I thought I would just point it out. I am sure there is a simple explanation to it. He testified at some length that he gave a statement in Belgrade. The prosecutors have represented to the court this afternoon that the Office of the Prosecutor was not welcome in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I'm sure there's a simple explanation, but before he is released, I think we ought to find out what's going on, just get this cleared up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He also said he made a statement in some international office. Maybe it's the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but what my question was -- is: Ms McHenry has this afternoon told the Tribunal -- I think her exact words were that the Office of the Prosecutor could not go to the FRY or was not allowed to go to the FRY, something like that. I'm sure there's some easy explanation but I would like to have it cleared up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly your Honours. We have no objection. At the time the statements were taken in Timosoira -- which was significantly before this witness was interviewed -- at that time the prosecution had not been permitted to go to the FRY to take statements. Subsequently the Office of the Prosecutor has been permitted to go within the FRY to take statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Like I said, your Honour, I was sure there was a simple explanation and I just got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would only like the previous statement of this witness to enter into evidence, since we don't believe it contains any inconsistency as to the very description of the interrogation inside the command building. So I would like to show the statement to the witness, ask him if he recognises his signature in it, then tender it for admission, and that would be all for my re-examination. May I ask that the witness be provided with the statement just to see whether he can recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you want additional material? Do you want something which has not come in cross-examination to be brought through re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This is exactly the statement that in all cross-examination was mentioned to a great extent, the previous statement done with Mr. McLeod in November 1996 in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I would object on two reasons. First, this exceeds the scope of cross. Secondly, the witness has testified, I think fairly clearly, that the interpretation is not reliable, and, given that, this is clearly not reliable evidence for purposes of the Tadic Decision. Again there's things -- the statement is full of things that nobody talked about on cross-examination. It clearly goes outside the scope of cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean the statement given to Mr. McLeod? It was touched many times in cross-examination. If I may add some argument, we are trying to do this, because, for instance, in his cross-examination Mr. Greaves made some generalisations and characterisations about what was said, but did not state exactly what was said. So for the record to be accurate and complete, we believe the statement to be useful and that it should be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How is that possible? You want to bring something new in re-examination. This does not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It's only to be considered for purposes of showing the extent to which -- it's not really a statement through which this witness can be really impeached on what he said -- for instance, when describing the very interrogation he had inside the command building -- and this arises directly out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it does. We can see the reliability of this past statement is being questioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Whether what he has said in the Trial Chamber today is different from what he said in his statement has been challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The reliability of the statement is not being

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: the witness. He is the one who said the statement is not reliable, not us. This is totally improper at this point. If Mr. Turone wanted this statement in evidence, then it should have been offered at the beginning during his direct examination, because now we find ourselves in the position where brand new evidence is coming into this case that we should have the opportunity to conduct substantial additional cross-examination on. I want to cross-examine him about every statement in there now as to whether the translator got it right or wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: When you were putting those discrepancies to him, you had the statement with you. You are mentioning discrepancies in those statements from what he said to the Trial Chamber. You knew about them, but actually it was not in evidence at the time you were raising those points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I wish to qualify now. Are you relying upon the statement which is made in this court today or the statement which he made before the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We are trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think there is a difference. For example, Mr. Ackerman pointed out about Klimenta's death. In that statement he said he was lying inside. Today he said he was standing at the door. On which are you relying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there might be simply some misunderstanding and some misinterpretation of the words in the statement. This is why I believe if the statement does not enter into evidence your Honours would never be able to control whether actually there is an inconsistency or not. Anyway, we are relying on what the witness said today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And not the statement which he made before the investigator. It is not his substantive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Then why are you producing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just because -- as I said, for instance, concerning the real -- the very description of the interrogation inside the command building, when there was a pistol, etc, Mr. Greaves made some characterisations about what was said but did not state exactly what was said. So for the record to be accurate and complete, we believe the statement must be admitted for this reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, he is taking the position that a seven-page statement that contains things that nobody has talked about in this courtroom at all today is admissible for all purposes because Mr. Greaves did not read a statement that supposedly impeached this witness. It just opens up the door. I know if this entire statement comes in I have at least another two hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think perhaps you might have changed your mind. Initially all that happened was this witness was contradicted by what he said in his previous statement and with some other statements about which perhaps there were doubts whether they were available or not. It appears there was an existing statement on the basis of which he was contradicted on what he said before the Trial Chamber. So if there is an opportunity of correcting that particular contradiction, then it is good for the Trial Chamber to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, like I say, my position is this is a seven-page statement. I am going through picking things at random.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You need not have relied on it even in your cross-examination if you did not talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
