utterances.text: Like I say, your Honour, there are substantial things in here that were not the subject of either direct or cross-examination that are just totally -- have nothing to do with anything that this man said today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: There are things he said there which were not said here today and that was pointed out. There are areas where he has gone further, which he did not read today, but areas where he described as being a wrong interpretation or not even a correct interpretation of what happened, which might have been misreported by the interpreter. These were all pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and that's the best reasons I can think of for excluding this document from evidence. If there is perchance some part of the document that I mischaracterised the contents of, or Mr. Greaves mischaracterised the contents of, or Mr. Ackerman mischaracterised the contents of, then clearly that's a proper subject for re-examination, but, given the fact that this clearly exceeds the scope of cross, and, two, is a document which the witness says is not a reliable document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has to make up its mind on what is the evidence before it. These are two contradicting areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think as I understand it, this man has been asked on cross-examination: "Did you make this statement?" He said: "No, I sure didn't". He says: "That's a misinterpretation". Okay. At that point the full statement that was in question, that portion of the statement, was placed before the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber clearly has before it sufficient information to determine whether or not this statement was made. It will not get any more by having the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I understand you. Traditionally when a statement is directly challenged by the defence you do it that way, but when out of your cross-examination there is an inference that he has made something contradictory to what he has stated in the Trial Chamber, the prosecution is entitled to correct that inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I concur completely with the court. What I'm saying to the court is this entire statement doesn't go in. If Mr. Turone in re-direct wants to go and clear that up and say: "Didn't you tell Mr. McLeod back on November 11th 1996 this?", I have no problem with that. What I have is this seven-page document -- I've got a problem with the seven-page document that's not the subject of cross-examination, that the witness says is unreliable, coming in as evidence before the Trial Chamber, the actual paper, not those portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will he now say it is reliable?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Beats the heck out of me, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Will he now say it is reliable? If in his evidence-in-chief he said certain things stated in there were not reliable, can he now say they are reliable? It is only those things which were stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, your Honour, I think my objection is clear. I am not objecting to Mr. Turone clearing up things in cross-examination and using the statement. I think that's perfectly proper for him to do. There's no question about that. The problem I have and I think the problem Mr. Ackerman has is that when we stick an exhibit tag on this thing and the Prosecutor moves to introduce this piece of paper into evidence, then he is anticipating going well outside the scope of cross, well outside the scope of his own re-direct and attempting to deprive us of our right to cross-examine and confront this witness. As long as it is limited and it is done orally like we were doing, I have absolutely no problem with him saying: "Well, isn't it true that you made a prior consistent statement to something?" That's fine. It's just the whole document doesn't come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear him, what he wants to introduce it for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the key to resolving this is very, very simple from an evidentiary standpoint. The Prosecutor said in response to Judge Jan's question: "Are you relying on the statement or on the testimony of the witness?", the Prosecutor said: "We're relying on the testimony of the witness, not on the statement". Ergo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Therefore he doesn't have to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ergo the statement is unreliable. Ergo the statement does not have any probative value and should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Not only in theory, in practice where a statement has been challenged through cross-examination or it was not presented to the witness himself, it is possible to introduce it in order to correct the impression that it was not properly made, that the statement itself does not contain what it says. It could be. But if the argument which it is now here is that the prosecution says he is not relying on it, then they need not actually from the beginning have wanted to put it in, because if he was relying on it also, then it becomes necessary for him to discuss whether it should enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Just also to clarify at least, I think, my position: when I say "reliability of the statement", I don't mean that I agree with the truth of the words in the statement, okay, but what I'm saying is it is my position that the interpreter for the Office of the Prosecutor properly interpreted what this man said, but I'm not challenging the reliability of the statement. I think that the Office of the Prosecutor and its interpreters perform their duties as they're supposed to, and I think there's an assumption under the law that public officials perform their duties like they're supposed to. It's this witness that has challenged the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: His own statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, he has challenged the -- whether the Office of the Prosecutor and its interpreters properly exercise their duties as public figures. I haven't done that. I don't think anybody up here has done that on the defence side. It would be my position that, regardless of the overall truth or falsity of the words on this paper, that they are the words that he spoke in Belgrade in November of 1996 and that were interpreted for Mr. -- whatever his name is -- the investigator, Mr. McLeod, and they were properly typed out, and that it was properly read back to this witness and that he could have made any corrections. I just don't think -- I can't stand here in good faith and tell you that the Office of the Prosecutor, its investigator and its interpreter are trying to pull a fast one on anybody. I think they're doing their job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Where I personally part ways with you is that you could not introduce a statement in re-examination. You could, depending on what was involved in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- I don't think we're parting ways. I think it is just an extent. I don't think that the whole thing comes in. I think just portions of it that were dealt with on cross-examination. It would be the relevant parts and other parts of it would not be relevant or probative of anything. Somebody needs to go through with a black marker and black it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not a toothcomb here. At least what he would perhaps have done is indicate those areas which are read in cross-examination and then indicate what he wants to do with that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are in perfect agreement that Mr. Turone needs to go forward a little bit, but I think that -- I think let us let him go forward and see what he wants to do rather than put in the entire statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Since the matter has been raised concerning my cross-examination, can I say this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was very careful to put one and only one specific point to the witness that he had not dealt with in his statement. I did not go -- and quite deliberately did not go beyond that incident concerning the pistol. My learned friend is entitled to ask those questions which arose from cross-examination. I very carefully sought to prevent him having that opportunity by the questions being put carefully about the pistol and the pistol only. In my respectful submission what he is trying to do is get evidence that he could not get out of his witness in the first place in by the back door. That's an improper use of re-examination, in my respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I respond, your Honour? I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I would like to insist that if we are seeking to enter into evidence this paper, it's not for the -- not as evidence for the truth of the matters which are written in this paper, only to help the Trial Chamber to determine the extent to which the witness has impeached in part this document and has not been impeached himself. Anyway, since this -- I understand it is a typical common law issue. Let me ask Ms McHenry to add some argument, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will be very brief. I think, in fact, that there is not necessarily a large amount of disagreement here. The defence attorneys attempted to impeach this witness with the statement. They did not, however, for instance, state exactly what the witness had said such that there are some -- and the witness himself was not presented with it and, in fact, doesn't even read the language. So there are some things that, in fact, can very well be explained. An example is when, for instance, the witness says about Mr. Keljo: "He was killed by Padalovic in front of the hangar, and the small door beside which I was lying was open, so I could see this." Defence counsel impeached him with this. Certainly the prosecution would like the actual words to be in there. For instance, there could be an argument about this can clearly be seen as a possible interpretation issue, and the small door besides which this witness was normally lying. It doesn't necessarily read it, especially when you see the detail of the seven pages. The defence counsel also attempted to impeach him generally and say: "All you do is talk about Delic". In fact, when you look at the statement as a whole, you can also see that he talks about other people. The prosecution is not trying to bring this into evidence for things other than what this witness testified. We are relying on the witness's testimony but to the extent that the defence attorneys have all, other than the Delalic defence which did not cross-examine -- since the defence attorneys have all attempted to impeach him, the document should be admitted solely for the purposes of determining to what extent, if any, the witness has been impeached. Now, it may be that in certain jury systems you would have to do it a different way and go through the entire statement and discuss this in great length and ask for an interpretation and then ask this. In front of your Honours, your Honours can consider evidence for only limited purposes. Certainly we believe that this Chamber can -- and in other trials I believe this has happened -- consider this statement just to the extent to which it does and it does not impeach him. In fact, previously defence counsel have introduced statements for that purpose and they are considered for impeachment, and, to the extent that the defence has attempted to do this but does not actually have the impeaching document, the prosecution is certainly entitled to present the entire document to your Honours, so your Honours can look at it and say: "Yes, he has been impeached about this", or, "I don't believe so." It is entirely appropriate and, in fact, in the long run more accurate and will save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why can't we have it for the purpose of impeachment only?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why can't we have it on the record for the purposes of impeachment only?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this: first, the Tadic Decision that we have beaten to death over the months says that evidence has to be, one, reliable, and, two, relevant. Let me just toss this out as a hypothetical to the court. The second to last paragraph in this thing says: "While at Musala some of the prisoners, including myself, were sent for labour", and then it continues. What in the world is that relevant to? It doesn't have anything to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is why I said only for the purposes of impeachment. You have impeached his credibility on the base of a certain statement. The prosecution wants that statement to be brought into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me first say that Ms McHenry has made the statement that in certain jury systems we do certain things. In fact, in the jury systems that I'm used to, and it may very well not be the systems in other countries, judges will regularly instruct jurors: "You will consider it for this purpose and not for that purpose." We have an appellate presumption that jurors follow their instructions. That aside, we also have non-jury proceedings on a fairly regular basis, and in these non-jury proceedings we use the same Rules of Evidence that we do when there's a jury sitting there. The only difference is that instead of having 12 people sitting in a corner, we have one judge sitting on a bench. The prosecution seems to be taking the position that because we have three judges rather than 12 jurors that we don't need any Rules of Evidence. I think the Tribunal has taken a rather different position in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence that we do need some kinds of Rules of Evidence, that there is no reason why, if the Prosecutor thinks this man has been impeached on one specific area, they can say: "Well, didn't you make a prior consistent statement, a prior statement that's consistent with what you said today? Didn't you tell Mr. McLeod this?" If they think that will rehabilitate him, that's fine with me. I don't have a problem with that. What I have a problem with is taking a document that that man sitting in the witness stand says is an unreliable document, and it's full of things that he hasn't talked about up here, so that the prosecution can get in front of the Trial Chamber things that they could not get out of their own witness, things that either aren't relevant or maybe are relevant but they never even attempted to get them out. They very easily could be things that the Prosecutor thinks are unreliable themselves or untrue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You see, we have a problem. We find we have to determine how far your attempted impeachment of the witness is successful. Unless we have the original statement before us and also the statement which is made before the court, how can we give any decision on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is why I say for the purpose of impeachment we should have the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will hear Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I will be as quick as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I should say everything goes back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour is most kind. Without conceding the generality you have placed and my opposition to learned friend's application, if the conclusion you came to was you ought to see the statement for the purposes only of impeachment, I would go on to submit this: you would only be entitled to have the passages upon which the cross-examination has taken place, because those other passages upon which cross-examination have not taken place have had no part in the case at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have to look at the entire statement and read the particular portions in the entire context of the document, not particularly that you cut out a few sentences and say: "This is what he means."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is a degree of context to be considered. Then let us say the man goes on to a completely different incident that has no bearing on the matters cross-examined about, you ought not to see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not substantive evidence in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me explain a little bit. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Whichever way you look at it, whether the evidence is reliable or relevant is determined by the Trial Chamber. It is a Trial Chamber. You might have your own views about it, but when the Trial Chamber considers a statement before it and the subject matter in respect of which it is considering that statement, whether that statement is relevant and in view of what we are considering, whether it is reliable depends on how we look at it as a whole. So it's not enough for you -- perhaps in preparing your case you might exclude it as not relevant, but somebody else might not think so. Somebody else might think it is relevant. But we decide, taking everything together, whether a particular thing is relevant and reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would completely agree that I'm an advocate and you're not. You, being the Trial Chamber, have the -- the obligation is to sort out these disputes between the parties. With that I very well understand that, and the Trial Chamber is well aware of my position and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We do. This is a Chamber which determines justice between the two parties. Nobody has to suffer merely because of ignorance of any of us. Perhaps if we are ignorant, a higher chamber might decide that, but definitely in this respect we think we could not allow a yawning gap that exists unless those statements which are necessary to inform us to accept what was said or not is in evidence. So we are not considering everything said in that statement, but those areas which affect the evidence given. Those are the things that concern us. In that regard we are entitled to accept the statement for the purpose. So we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, admit it just for that limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of impeachment and not as substantive evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure the record is clear on that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is the purpose. It wasn't being challenged that that was not his evidence. Nobody has challenged that, but there are areas which are in conflict with what he said before us. Yes, Ms Residovic? MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, I take it that you have not passed the Ruling until you hear all of our arguments. I have tried a number of times to take the floor, but my colleagues were quicker than me. I know that the Trial Chamber will take as the basis the testimony of this witness uttered before this Trial Chamber, but to admit a seven-page statement mentioning events and facts which were not the subject of the main examination, nor of the cross-examination, without limiting the text to only those questions which were referred to in this Trial Chamber and which were the subject of both the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination would mean improper offering of evidence to this trial Chamber, and I think no Trial Chamber, and especially not this one, could accept it. The basis of the decision of Mr. Delalic's defence not to do any cross-examination was based on the statement made by this witness in the Trial Chamber. I don't know whether our defence counsel would have made the same defence if the Prosecutor had offered the statement during the examination-in-chief, nor during the cross-examination. That is why I propose that this statement should be limited to the number of pages covering the issues which were raised in the course of the examination-in-chief and cross-examination, in other words that it be redacted in such a way, and only then, after it has been redacted, can it be admitted for the reasons you have given. If there is any intention to offer as evidence something that was not discussed in this courtroom, because the Prosecutor failed to raise those issues before the court in any other way, then I think we are entitled to additional cross-examination. That is why I think, according to any law, and in the interests of justice, this statement that is being tendered as evidence needs to be redacted for the reasons I have given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I have outlined the principles under which we are admitting the statement. Apart from that, it is not only to have irrelevancies in cross-examination which are part of the record. So if there are irrelevance seems -- in the statement, which have nothing to do with the purpose for which it is being admitted -- it will not be taken into consideration at all. It is our duty to be of service and fair to everyone who is concerned here and not to remove any particular matters merely because a particular counsel doesn't like it that way. I think that would be unfair even to the counsel and to the other persons concerned. We will admit it for the purpose for which it has been submitted. That is for contradictory statements which appear before the Trial Chamber. Now what is the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is number 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have no other questions for re-examination, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that's all you have for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Just before you decide how to handle the next witness, I have one small point to make that may affect your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Still with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, not for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness is discharged and he can now go away. He can go. (Witness withdrew from court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think what we have before us here, is this a motion for protective measures for witness B? Is that what you want to speak about. 1 2 3 4 5 6
